summary: Lamentations 'all her splendor has gone' is interpreted as the cheruvim facing each other (symbol of divine love) being exposed at the Temple's destruction. R. Yehuda teaches that the world's ends converge in Jerusalem. The Gemara then presents traditions about the Ark: R. Eliezer says it was taken to Babylon; R. Shimon ben Yochai says it is hidden under the Temple. The HP's service in the Second Temple was performed toward the even ha-shetiya regardless.

display.whats: The verse 'all her splendor has gone' and how the cheruvim in the Holy of Holies were facing each other
display.hint: Lamentations says 'all her splendor has gone.' The Gemara interprets this: when the Temple was destroyed, the cheruvim on the Ark were seen facing each other (as in times of divine favor), yet God had abandoned it. R. Yehuda notes the world's extremities meet in Jerusalem.
display.title: Cheruvim Facing Each Other as a Sign of Divine Favor

learning.ahaMoment: The cheruvim facing each other symbolized divine-Israel intimacy. Their exposure during destruction was the ultimate violation of sacred privacy.
learning.memoryAnchor: Cheruvim facing each other = divine love; their exposed intimacy at destruction = Israel's deepest humiliation.
learning.learnerQuestion: What did the position of the cheruvim on the Ark indicate about the relationship between God and Israel, and how was this visible to people?
learning.coreTension: The cheruvim were in the Holy of Holies, normally unseen; yet the Talmud connects their facing position to the state of the divine-human relationship. The question is how this private indicator became a public sign.
learning.coreMove: The Talmud teaches that when the cheruvim faced each other, it was a sign of divine favor and love - like two people facing each other in intimacy. When Israel would sin, the cheruvim would turn away. Pilgrims were shown this during festivals as testimony to God's love.

takeaway.text: The cheruvim facing each other was a sign of divine favor and love toward Israel; the Talmud records that pilgrims were shown this during festivals as living testimony that God cherished the Jewish people.

learning.learningBlocker: Students may find it strange that something inside the Holy of Holies was shown to pilgrims; the disclosure of the cheruvim's position during festivals is not obvious from the usual descriptions of Temple access.

misconceptions.misconception: The cheruvim facing each other was a sign of disfavor or tension, like two adversaries facing off.
misconceptions.correction: The cheruvim facing each other represented divine love and favor toward Israel, like two people facing each other in closeness and affection; pilgrims were shown this as evidence of God's enduring love.

quizSeeds.answer: The cheruvim facing each other symbolized divine intimacy and love. Their exposed intimate posture at the moment of destruction shows that even in the moment God allowed destruction, the love persisted - yet was violated by the gentiles' intrusion.
quizSeeds.question: What is the significance of the cheruvim facing each other at the Temple's destruction?

sugyot.finalRuling: The cheruvim facing each other symbolized divine love; their exposed intimacy at destruction was Israel's deepest humiliation and paradoxically, a sign of God's enduring love.

display.whats: Where was the Ark hidden? Various traditions about its location
display.hint: The Gemara presents multiple traditions about where the Ark was hidden: under the Temple, in a cave in Beit Shemesh, carried to Babylon, or hidden elsewhere. The Mishna preserves the tradition that it was hidden by the Sages of Josiah's generation.
display.title: Ark Fate Traditions and the Second Temple Sprinkling Target

learning.ahaMoment: Multiple traditions about the Ark's hiding place reflect its supreme importance - people preserved traditions about it even when they could not verify them.
learning.memoryAnchor: Where is the Ark? Babylon (R. Eliezer) or under the Temple (R. Shimon ben Yochai). Both preserve hope of finding it.
learning.learnerQuestion: Given the various traditions about what happened to the Ark, does uncertainty about the Ark's fate undermine the validity of the Second Temple Yom Kippur service?
learning.coreTension: Multiple traditions exist about the Ark: that it was hidden by Josiah, taken to Babylon, or stored in a chamber. The blood sprinkling requires a specific target location; if the Ark's fate is uncertain, so might be the sprinkling target.
learning.coreMove: The Talmud resolves this by establishing that regardless of what happened to the Ark, the even ha-shetiya marks the precise spot where the Ark stood. The HP sprinkles on or toward that spot in all cases, making the sprinkling target stable despite Ark-fate uncertainty.

takeaway.text: Regardless of which tradition about the Ark's fate is correct, the even ha-shetiya marks the permanent location of the Ark's original position; the High Priest always sprinkles toward that spot, making the ritual independent of the Ark's actual fate.

learning.learningBlocker: Students may assume that the Second Temple Yom Kippur service was somehow incomplete or invalid because the Ark was missing; the Talmud establishes that the spatial location was always the true target.

rashiTranslations.en: 'All her chamber' - hidden away in the innermost chambers. 'Fifty-two years' - this was from the destruction of Jerusalem in Zedekiah's exile until Cyrus's decree, when they went up to build the House, since at the end of seventy years from the exile of

Jehoiakim was the decree, as we learned in Megillah (11b); and it was eighteen years from the conquest of Jehoiakim until the destruction of Jerusalem, as the master said: they went into exile in the seventh year, in the eighth year, they went

into exile in the eighteenth year, they went into exile in the nineteenth year; and its explanation is: Jeconiah went into exile in the seventh year of Jehoiakim's conquest, which is the eighth year of Nebuchadnezzar; Zedekiah's exile, at the destruction of Jerusalem, was in the eighteenth
year of Jehoiakim's conquest, which is the nineteenth of Nebuchadnezzar, as the master said: in the first year he conquered Nineveh, in the second he went up and conquered Jehoiakim. 'Until beast' -
'beast' in gematria is fifty-two. 'He strengthened'
'for the many' - it is written in the book of Daniel, and thus
Rabbi Yochanan explains it: that 'covenant' stated
regarding sulfur and salt, of which it is said, 'because
they forsook the covenant' - 'he strengthened' means the enemy prevailed over
Israel for one week. 'For the many' - for the officers,
as in 'all the officers of the king of Babylon' (Jeremiah 39).
'He occupied himself' - in strolling and playing. 'A pavement
tile different' - one of the marble tiles
in the pavement he saw was higher than its fellows, and he understood
that it had been removed after it had been set there.
'With certainty' - clearly. 'They were checking the wood for worms' -
as we learned (Middot 2:5): any wood that has
a worm in it is unfit for the altar. 'Blemished priests' -
who are not fit for other service. 'Visible
and not visible' - as is explained further in the beraita,
that they pressed against and bulged out through the curtain and appeared
like a woman's two breasts, which bulge out from beneath
her garment. 'And emerge through the curtain' - the one spread
opposite the doorway in the partition of the amah-width screen wall,
and the doorway was in the middle of the amah-width screen wall
in the First Temple. 'The cheruvim' - joined
to each other, holding and embracing one another
like a male embracing a female. 'Intertwined' -
an expression of clinging, as in (Uktzin 3:8),
'a tree that was split but remains attached by its bark,' and in tractate
Beitza (7a): 'if they were attached by sinews
they are forbidden.' 'And they shall not come to see' - the Levites
in the wilderness, even though they carried
the sacred vessels on their shoulders, were not permitted
to enter at the time the camps journeyed onward, when
they dismantled the Ark and the altar to move it
from its place, until Aaron and his sons covered
it in its coverings, as is written in the portion,
'and they shall cover it with a covering of tachash hide, and take
a cloth of blue and cover' etc. 'As it is swallowed' is a term of
covering. 'In her father's house' - during her betrothal, even
Israel in the wilderness were not yet overly familiar
with the Divine Presence. 'You mean when she was divorced' - this
incident took place in the Second Temple, after they had been divorced
and had returned. 'To her first love' - to the beginning of
their love, when they were not overly familiar with one another. 'With what
are we dealing' - this 'they would roll up the curtain for them
and show them the cheruvim.' 'Were there
cheruvim' - since one might think this refers to the cheruvim that
Solomon made beside the Ark, on this side and that, is what is meant.
'Of the doorways' - which were opposite the entrances: the entrance of the Entrance Hall,
the Sanctuary, and the Holy of Holies. 'Thirteen
curtains there were in the Second Temple' -
seven for the seven gates of the courtyard, two
at the innermost sanctuary in place of the amah-width screen wall,
and two corresponding to them on the outside, between the upper chamber of
the Sanctuary and the upper chamber of the Holy of Holies,
and just as in the Second Temple there were curtains
opposite the doorways, so too in
the First Temple. 'Cheruvim of form' -
painted on the wall with dyes, or carved into the wooden walls in front of the stone walls. 'Surrounded with carved-work' - designs of latticework and carvings.
'Like a man' - the comment is completed on 54b.
